keywords.definition: The processor: the component that carries out instructions by repeatedly fetching, decoding and executing them.
The part of the processor that carries out arithmetic operations (such as addition and subtraction) and logical operations (such as AND, OR and comparisons) on data.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Control Unit: decodes instructions and coordinates the processor; it doesn't do the calculations.

keywords.definition: The part of the processor that decodes instructions and sends control signals to coordinate the other components and the movement of data into, out of and within the processor.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: ALU: performs the arithmetic and logic; the Control Unit directs it.

keywords.definition: A small, very fast storage location inside the processor that holds an instruction, a memory address or an item of data while it is being used.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Cache: also fast memory on the processor, but holds copies of frequently used instructions and data from RAM rather than the value being worked on right now.

keywords.definition: A register that holds the memory address of the next instruction to be fetched.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: MAR: holds the address of the memory location currently being read from or written to.

keywords.definition: A register that holds the data currently being processed and stores the results of calculations carried out by the ALU.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: MDR: holds data on its way to or from memory; the ACC holds the value being worked on and the ALU's result.

keywords.definition: A register that holds the address of the memory location currently being read from or written to.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: MDR: holds the data or instruction itself, not its address.

keywords.definition: A register that holds the data or instruction that has just been read from memory, or that is about to be written to memory.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: MAR: holds the address of the memory location, not the data stored there.

keywords.definition: A register that holds the instruction currently being decoded and executed.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: PC: holds the address of the next instruction, not the current instruction itself.

keywords.definition: A set of parallel wires that carries signals between the components of a computer, such as between the processor and memory.
A bidirectional bus that carries data and instructions between the processor, memory and input/output devices.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Address bus: carries memory addresses, one way only, from the processor to memory.

keywords.definition: A unidirectional bus that carries memory addresses from the processor to memory; its width determines how many memory locations can be addressed.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Data bus: carries the data and instructions themselves, in both directions.

keywords.definition: A bidirectional bus that carries control signals, such as memory read, memory write and clock signals, between the control unit and the other components.
The cycle the processor repeats for every instruction: fetch the next instruction from memory, decode it to work out what to do, then execute it.
The number of clock cycles the processor carries out per second, measured in hertz (Hz); a higher clock speed means more instructions can be executed each second.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Number of cores: more cores lets more instructions run at the same time; clock speed is how fast each core works through them.

keywords.definition: An independent processing unit within a processor that can fetch, decode and execute instructions on its own.
A small amount of very fast memory in or next to the processor that stores frequently used instructions and data, so they can be accessed more quickly than from RAM.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: RAM: main memory; much larger but slower to access than cache.

keywords.definition: Overlapping the stages of the FDE cycle, so that while one instruction is being executed the next is being decoded and the one after that is being fetched.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Parallel processing: separate cores or processors working at the same time; pipelining overlaps the stages of different instructions within one processor.

keywords.definition: A processor architecture in which instructions and data are stored in the same memory and travel along the same buses, so they can't be fetched at the same time.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Harvard architecture: separate memories and buses for instructions and data.

keywords.definition: A processor architecture with physically separate memories and buses for instructions and data, so an instruction and an item of data can be accessed at the same time.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Von Neumann architecture: one shared memory and set of buses for both.

keywords.definition: Modern processors combine both designs: instructions and data share main memory (Von Neumann), but the processor has separate caches for instructions and for data (Harvard).
A processor design with a large set of complex instructions, some taking several clock cycles, so a task needs fewer lines of assembly code.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: RISC: a small set of simple instructions, each typically taking one clock cycle.

keywords.definition: A processor design with a small set of simple instructions, each typically completed in one clock cycle, which makes pipelining easier.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: CISC: many complex instructions, some taking several clock cycles.

keywords.definition: A processor with a large number of cores designed to carry out the same operation on many items of data at the same time, used for graphics and other highly parallel tasks such as modelling and data mining.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: CPU: fewer, more powerful cores suited to general-purpose and sequential tasks.

keywords.definition: Processing in which one instruction is carried out on many items of data at the same time.
A processor with two or more cores on a single chip, so several instructions, or several programs, can be processed at the same time.
Using two or more processors or cores at the same time to carry out different parts of a task, or different tasks.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Pipelining: overlaps the stages of instructions inside one processor rather than using several processors.

keywords.definition: Hardware used to enter data into a computer system, such as a keyboard, barcode scanner, microphone or sensor.
Hardware used to present the results of processing to a person or another system, such as a monitor, printer, speaker or actuator.
Non-volatile storage that holds programs and data that are not currently in use, such as a hard disk drive, SSD or optical disc.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: RAM: main memory holding what is in use right now, and volatile.

keywords.definition: Storage that records data by magnetising tiny areas of a spinning disk or a tape in one of two directions, such as a hard disk drive or magnetic tape.
Storage that uses a laser to read (and on some discs write) data on the reflective surface of a disc, such as a CD, DVD or Blu-ray.
Solid-state, non-volatile storage that holds data electronically in memory chips with no moving parts, such as an SSD, USB memory stick or SD card.
Volatile main memory that holds the programs and data currently in use, and can be both read from and written to.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: ROM: non-volatile and normally read-only; holds start-up instructions.

keywords.definition: Non-volatile memory whose contents cannot normally be changed, used to store the instructions needed to start the computer, such as the BIOS.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: RAM: volatile, read/write memory for programs and data in use.

keywords.definition: Describes memory that loses its contents when the power is switched off, such as RAM.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Non-volatile: keeps its contents without power.

keywords.definition: Describes memory or storage that keeps its contents when the power is switched off, such as ROM, flash and magnetic storage.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Volatile: loses its contents without power.

keywords.definition: Storage that may appear to be local but is physically located elsewhere on the network, remotely or in the cloud.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Virtual memory (1.2.1): part of secondary storage used as if it were extra RAM when RAM is full.

keywords.definition: System software that manages the computer's hardware and resources and provides a platform and user interface for running other software.
The part of the operating system that allocates memory to processes, keeps them separate from each other, and moves data between RAM and secondary storage when needed.
Dividing memory into fixed-size blocks called pages, so a program's pages can be stored in any free page frames in memory, not necessarily next to each other.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Segmentation: divides memory into variable-size blocks based on the logical parts of a program.

keywords.definition: Dividing memory into variable-size blocks called segments, each holding a logical part of a program such as a subroutine or a data structure.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Paging: fixed-size pages, divided physically rather than by what the program contains.

keywords.definition: An area of secondary storage used as if it were extra RAM when RAM is full; pages not currently needed are swapped out to it and swapped back in when required.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Virtual storage (1.1.3): storage located elsewhere on a network or in the cloud.

keywords.definition: When the computer spends more time swapping pages between RAM and virtual memory than running programs, so it slows down badly.
A signal to the processor from hardware or software saying that something needs attention, which may cause the processor to stop its current task and run an interrupt service routine.
The code that runs to deal with a particular interrupt; afterwards, the saved state of the interrupted task is restored and it carries on.
How the operating system decides which process gets processor time next, so that time is shared fairly and efficiently between processes.
A scheduling algorithm that gives each process a fixed time slice in turn; a process that hasn't finished goes to the back of the queue.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: First come first served: each process runs to completion before the next one starts; no time slices.

keywords.definition: A scheduling algorithm that runs processes in the order they arrive, each one to completion before the next starts.
A scheduling algorithm that uses several queues of different priority, moving processes between queues according to how they behave (for example, how much processor time they use).
A scheduling algorithm that runs the waiting process with the shortest estimated total running time next, letting it run to completion.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Shortest remaining time: can interrupt the running process when a shorter one arrives.

keywords.definition: A scheduling algorithm that always runs the process with the least time left to finish, switching to a newly arrived process if it would finish sooner.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Shortest job first: once a job starts, it runs to completion.

keywords.definition: An operating system that runs across several computers and makes them appear to the user as a single system, sharing tasks and resources between them.
A small operating system built into a dedicated device, such as a washing machine or car engine controller, designed for a specific task with limited resources.
An operating system that appears to run several programs at the same time by switching the processor between them very quickly.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Multi-user operating system: lets several users use the computer's resources at once.

keywords.definition: An operating system that allows several users to use one computer's resources at the same time, using scheduling to share processor time fairly between them.
An operating system that guarantees to process inputs and respond within a fixed, very short time, used where delays could be dangerous, such as in aircraft or medical equipment.
Firmware stored in ROM that runs when the computer is switched on: it checks the hardware (POST), then loads the operating system's boot loader from storage.
Software that lets the operating system communicate with a particular hardware device by translating the operating system's general instructions into ones the device understands.
Software that takes on the function of a machine, for example running an operating system inside another, or executing intermediate code.
Code that is partly translated (such as bytecode) and can be run on any platform that has a suitable virtual machine to execute it.
Software that lets the user carry out a task, such as a word processor, web browser, database or graphics editor.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Utility software: maintains or improves the running of the computer rather than doing the user's task.

keywords.definition: System software that performs a specific task to maintain or improve the running of the computer, such as disk defragmentation, backup, compression or anti-virus.
Software whose source code is made freely available, so users can view, modify and redistribute it under its licence.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Closed source: only the compiled program is supplied and the source code is kept private.

keywords.definition: Software whose source code is kept private by its owner; users get only the compiled program and a licence that restricts how they can use it.
A program that converts source code into machine code: a compiler, an interpreter or an assembler.
A translator that converts the whole of a high-level program into machine code (object code) in one go, producing an executable that can be run without the compiler.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Interpreter: translates and runs the program one line at a time, every time it runs.

keywords.definition: A translator that translates and executes a high-level program one line at a time, stopping at the first error it finds.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Compiler: translates the whole program once and produces an executable file.

keywords.definition: A translator that converts assembly language into machine code, generally one machine code instruction for each assembly language instruction.
A program as written by the programmer in a programming language, before it is translated.
The machine code produced by translating source code, which may still need to be linked with library code before it can run.
Instructions in binary that the processor can execute directly.
The first stage of compilation: comments and whitespace are removed and the source code is split into tokens, with identifiers added to a symbol table.
The smallest meaningful unit of source code, such as a keyword, identifier, operator or value, produced by lexical analysis.
A table built during compilation that records each identifier (such as a variable or subroutine name) with information about it, such as its data type and scope.
The stage of compilation that checks the tokens follow the rules (grammar) of the language, reports any syntax errors, and builds an abstract syntax tree.
A tree representing the structure of the program, built during syntax analysis and passed on to code generation.
The stage of compilation that produces object code (machine code) from the abstract syntax tree.
The stage of compilation that changes the code so it runs faster or uses less memory, without changing what it does, for example by removing redundant instructions.
A collection of pre-written, pre-tested code (such as subroutines) that programmers can use in their own programs.
A program that combines object code with the library code it uses into a single executable file.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Loader: copies the executable into memory so it can run.

keywords.definition: Part of the operating system that copies an executable program (and any dynamically linked libraries it needs) into memory so it can run.
Copying the library code a program needs into its executable file, which makes the file larger but means it runs without the library installed.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Dynamic linking: the library stays separate and is loaded when the program runs.

keywords.definition: Keeping library code in a separate file that is loaded when the program runs, so executables are smaller and many programs can share one copy of the library.
A software development model in which each stage (such as analysis, design, implementation, testing and maintenance) is completed in order before the next one begins.
Approaches to software development that build the software in short, repeated iterations, delivering working parts often and adapting to changing requirements through close contact with the client.
An agile methodology that develops software in short iterations using practices such as pair programming, test-first development and a customer representative working with the team.
An extreme programming practice in which two programmers work at one computer, one writing code while the other reviews it, swapping roles regularly.
A software development model that repeats a cycle of planning, risk analysis, development and evaluation, building a larger version of the software each loop; suited to large, high-risk projects.
A software development model that builds a series of prototypes quickly, getting user feedback on each one, until the prototype becomes the final product.
An early, incomplete version of a system built to show users how it will look and work and to get their feedback.
A sequence of steps that can be followed to solve a problem or complete a task.
A way of writing an algorithm using structured, code-like statements that are not tied to any particular programming language.
A diagram that shows an algorithm using standard symbols (such as start/stop, process, decision and input/output) connected by arrows.
A style or approach to programming, such as procedural, object-oriented or low-level, each suited to different kinds of problem.
A language in which a program is a sequence of instructions grouped into procedures and functions, using sequence, selection and iteration.
A language close to the processor's own instructions, such as machine code or assembly language, giving direct control of the hardware.
A low-level language that uses mnemonics in place of binary machine code instructions, usually with one mnemonic per machine code instruction.
A short, memorable code for a machine code instruction, such as ADD or LDA in assembly language.
A simplified model of a Von Neumann computer with a small instruction set, used to learn assembly language programming.
The part of a machine code or assembly language instruction that says which operation to carry out.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Operand: the data, or the address of the data, the operation works on.

keywords.definition: The part of an instruction that holds the data to be used, or the address of that data.
LMC instruction that adds the value stored at the given memory address to the accumulator.
LMC instruction that subtracts the value stored at the given memory address from the accumulator.
LMC instruction that copies the value in the accumulator into the given memory address.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: LDA: copies a value from memory into the accumulator (the opposite direction).

keywords.definition: LMC instruction that copies the value stored at the given memory address into the accumulator.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: STA: copies the accumulator into memory (the opposite direction).

keywords.definition: LMC instruction that always jumps to the given address, by setting the program counter to it.
LMC instruction that jumps to the given address only if the value in the accumulator is zero.
LMC instruction that jumps to the given address only if the value in the accumulator is zero or positive.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: BRZ: branches only when the accumulator is exactly zero.

keywords.definition: LMC instruction that takes a value from the user and stores it in the accumulator.
LMC instruction that outputs the value in the accumulator.
LMC instruction that stops the program.
LMC instruction that reserves a memory location (labelled) to hold data, optionally with a starting value.
The way an instruction's operand is interpreted to find the data: immediate, direct, indirect or indexed.
An addressing mode in which the operand is the actual value to be used.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Direct addressing: the operand is the address where the value is stored.

keywords.definition: An addressing mode in which the operand is the memory address of the value to be used.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Indirect addressing: the operand is the address of a location holding the address of the value.

keywords.definition: An addressing mode in which the operand is the address of a memory location that holds the address of the value to be used.
An addressing mode in which the address of the value is found by adding the operand to the value in the index register; useful for working through an array.
A register whose value is added to the operand in indexed addressing; incrementing it steps through consecutive memory locations.
A language in which programs are built from objects, created from classes, that combine data (attributes) with the code that acts on it (methods).
A template that defines the attributes and methods that objects of that type will have.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Object: a specific instance created from a class.

keywords.definition: An instance of a class, with its own values for the class's attributes.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Class: the template the object is created from.

keywords.definition: Creating an object from a class, which runs the class's constructor; in OCR pseudocode, for example, myDog = new Dog("Fido", "Scottish Terrier").
A method that runs when an object is created, used to set up its attributes; in OCR pseudocode it is a procedure called new.
A variable that belongs to a class or object and holds data about it.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Method: a subroutine that belongs to the class.

keywords.definition: A subroutine (procedure or function) that belongs to a class and defines a behaviour of its objects.
When a subclass takes on the attributes and methods of its superclass, and can add its own or override them.
A class whose attributes and methods are inherited by one or more subclasses; also called a parent class.
A class that inherits the attributes and methods of a superclass; also called a child class.
Keeping an object's attributes private so they can only be accessed or changed through its public methods, such as get and set methods.
An access level meaning an attribute or method can only be used from inside its own class.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Public: can be used from outside the class.

keywords.definition: An access level meaning an attribute or method can be used from outside its class; in OCR pseudocode, methods and attributes are public unless stated otherwise.
Public methods that return (get) or change (set) the value of a private attribute, so other code can't access the attribute directly.
The ability of objects of different classes to respond to the same method call in their own way, for example a subclass overriding a method it inherits.
A named value that cannot be changed while the program is running.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Variable: a named value that can change while the program runs.

keywords.definition: A named location in memory that holds a value which can change while the program is running.
